# AWS’s Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents’ mistakes

Earlier this month, the team behind Hydro developed a new way to check that a distributed system still works correctly when it resends messages after a failure.

This produced what Shadaj Laddad described to me as “like a 5000 line PR.” Hydro is an open-source Rust framework for distributed systems, the software that runs across many machines at once, and agents now write most of it with humans driving. The PR was difficult to split into smaller pieces as its components worked together.

That’s a lot of code to review for a tool developers count on to catch bugs. Laddad, research lead for the Hydro team at AWS, says it’s something the team spends a lot of time thinking about. I sat down with him last week at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose. He was set to give a keynote the next day where he was going to argue code review can’t keep pace with how agents write code.

Agents have let the team aim higher, Laddad told me, saying PRs arrive faster and run longer. “You can have the feature work well in isolation, then you mix it with something else, and suddenly the guarantees break down,” he said. And you can’t just trust the tests. In most agent workflows, he says, the agent writes both the code and the unit tests. “Agents are great, but they’re unpredictable,” Laddad said. That unpredictability is part of what makes them creative, and it makes it hard for a human to review all those tests and confirm they do what the team wants.

His answer is shared Correctness checks outside the agent’s “zone of trust,” such as those enforced by a compiler. Rust’s borrow checker is his example: It catches race conditions before the code ever runs. Hydro does something similar for distributed systems, catching several types of bugs at compile time so an agent gets instant feedback on mistakes it introduced. The wider goal, which the team is still exploring, is domain-specific guardrails that agents can share.

To find candidates, the team studies historical projects for recurring patterns. Idempotency, ensuring a retried request doesn’t run twice, comes up repeatedly in design reviews, so the team is asking whether it can become a general-purpose guardrail. Laddad sees this as the next rung on an old ladder. C spared programmers from mangling function calls in assembly. Java took memory allocation off their plate. Agents, he argued, make the next layer more urgent.

Compilers have limits, though. As The New Stack reported in August, AI-generated Rust can compile perfectly and still be wrong .

The same team also built Infinity , an open-source agent runtime AWS announced on October 23. It suspends an agent while it waits on a tool call or a CI job instead of keeping it running. Laddad cited a benchmark showing 75,000 concurrent agents on a single Raspberry Pi. According to the AWS announcement, that figure is extrapolated from a server test in which each idle agent used about 100 KB.

Hydro itself is an early release, built for teams running high-throughput, low-latency services who are constantly worried about distributed systems bugs. Laddad noted that users should expect rough edges and a learning curve right now. The payoff is the confidence to change a system without fearing it will break a few months later. Hydro and Infinity are open source at hydro.run , built jointly by AWS and UC Berkeley.

# What happens when the agent is long gone, but its access key lives on?

Imagine: There’s a line on the credential report that no one on the platform team can explain. An IAM user called research-agent-2 has an access key created 14 months ago that was last used 11 months ago. And it’s still active.

The project it supported closed long ago, and the person who approved it doesn’t even work at the company anymore.

While this example is hypothetical, the lifecycle problem isn’t.

This doesn’t require carelessness. An agent is created for a task, the task ends, and nobody revisits its access. A departing person triggers offboarding; a finished agent just leaves a closed tab. AWS IAM user access keys don’t expire automatically, so a forgotten key stays valid until somebody disables or deletes it.

> “A departing person triggers offboarding; a finished agent just leaves a closed tab.”

OWASP puts improper offboarding first in its 2025 Top 10 for non-human identities , and the remedy reads like this series’ premise: retire what’s no longer needed, and give the rest an accountable owner. The hard part is knowing what exists.

The problem is that attackers move faster than an annual audit ever could. In September 2026, GreyNoise documented an AI-orchestrated campaign against PaperCut servers: the attacker went from an empty workspace to remote code execution at a real victim in under four hours, and once launched, the campaign compromised at least eleven organizations in 26 seconds. That wasn’t an attack using abandoned AWS IAM keys. It shows how quickly exposed access becomes useful once an attacker is in, and why slow inventory and revocation are dangerous.

An agent’s access can outlive its purpose unless someone governs its lifecycle.

The last three articles covered attaching an owner at discovery , reassigning one before a last day , and what happens when the owner is an agent . Credentials add a related problem, with one distinction. An agent’s deployment identity is what authenticates it, or the deployment platform, to a cloud account.

> “A forgotten VM costs money; a forgotten credential can grant access.”

A provisioned credential is a persistent key, secret, or token that a deployment creates for some other workload; the two have different owners and revocation procedures. A forgotten VM costs money; a forgotten credential can grant access. The remedy is still a query, a policy, and a clock, each used for the part of the problem it can solve.

## 1. The query that finds keys no one is using

CloudQuery can sync AWS IAM credential reports into aws_iam_credential_reports when that table is enabled in the source configuration. The report lists up to two access-key slots per user. This query, written for the ClickHouse dialect CloudQuery Platform uses, takes the latest synced row for each report, turns the slots into rows, and returns active IAM user keys that are at least 90 days old and unused for at least 90 days.

SQL WITH latest_reports AS ( SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, `user` AS principal, access_key1_active, access_key_1_last_rotated, access_key_1_last_used_date, access_key2_active, access_key_2_last_rotated, access_key_2_last_used_date FROM aws_iam_credential_reports ORDER BY _cq_sync_group_id DESC, _cq_sync_time DESC LIMIT 1 BY _cq_platform_id ), keys AS ( SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal, 1 AS key_slot, access_key1_active AS active, access_key_1_last_rotated AS created, access_key_1_last_used_date AS last_used FROM latest_reports UNION ALL SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal, 2 AS key_slot, access_key2_active AS active, access_key_2_last_rotated AS created, access_key_2_last_used_date AS last_used FROM latest_reports ) SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal, key_slot, created, last_used FROM keys WHERE principal != '<root_account>' AND active = true AND created < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY AND ( last_used IS NULL OR last_used < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY ) ORDER BY last_used NULLS FIRST, principal, key_slot;

The active flags, access_key1_active and access_key2_active , have no underscore before the digit; the date columns do. On Platform, a table name already points at the latest complete snapshot , so the latest-row clause matters on destinations that keep history, where it can also resurface a user deleted since.

The 90-day window is a review threshold, not a verdict: quarterly jobs have quiet keys, and a null or placeholder last-used date means investigate, not “never needed.” The report doesn’t say which agent used an account; correlate with audit logs and a named owner. The query skips the root account, whose access keys need a separate, urgent audit; AWS recommends having none.

On PostgreSQL, quote "user" with double quotes, use interval '90 days' , and replace LIMIT 1 BY with DISTINCT ON . Here the ARN, which is unique per IAM user, identifies each report:

SQL WITH latest_reports AS ( SELECT DISTINCT ON (arn) arn, "user" AS principal, access_key1_active, access_key_1_last_rotated, access_key_1_last_used_date, access_key2_active, access_key_2_last_rotated, access_key_2_last_used_date FROM aws_iam_credential_reports ORDER BY arn, _cq_sync_time DESC ), keys AS ( SELECT arn, principal, 1 AS key_slot, access_key1_active AS active, access_key_1_last_rotated AS created, access_key_1_last_used_date AS last_used FROM latest_reports UNION ALL SELECT arn, principal, 2 AS key_slot, access_key2_active AS active, access_key_2_last_rotated AS created, access_key_2_last_used_date AS last_used FROM latest_reports ) SELECT split_part(arn, ':', 5) AS account_id, arn, principal, key_slot, created, last_used FROM keys WHERE principal <> '<root_account>' AND active AND created < now() - interval '90 days' AND (last_used IS NULL OR last_used < now() - interval '90 days') ORDER BY last_used NULLS FIRST, principal, key_slot;

The result is a prioritized review list. Next, the human question matters: who owns this credential, what still depends on it, and when should it stop working?

Other clouds raise the same concern elsewhere. In Entra ID, entraid_serviceprincipals includes credential metadata and entraid_serviceprincipal_owners shows who’s accountable; inspect identifiers and validity dates, not secret values, since Microsoft Graph returns secretText only at creation . In Google Cloud, gcp_iam_service_account_keys can inventory service-account keys if that table is enabled in your sync, but inventory alone doesn’t show use; check Google Cloud’s audit logs.

## 2. The policy that keeps agents from minting keys

The query cleans up what exists. An env zero approval policy can stop certain new keys at deploy time, but only where env zero governs the deployment: policies are enforced at deploy and destroy, not for credentials created in a console, by an external script, or by an env zero task, and they don’t revoke the identity authenticating a deployment. Cloud-native IAM controls, like an AWS service control policy or GCP’s organization policy for service account keys, and the inventory above still do that work.

Assign the policy to a project and every environment under it, subprojects included, inherits it. It doesn’t need to know whether a person or an agent clicked Deploy; it refuses selected long-lived credential types in Terraform and OpenTofu plans. Prefer federation where you can: env zero supports OIDC-based deployment authentication , and an AWS role issues temporary credentials that expire with the session, though the role itself doesn’t.

package env0 import future.keywords.contains import future.keywords.every import future.keywords.if import future.keywords.in key_resources := { "aws_iam_access_key", "aws_iam_user_login_profile", "aws_iam_service_specific_credential", "aws_iam_signing_certificate", "google_service_account_key", "azuread_service_principal_password", "azuread_application_password", "azuread_service_principal_certificate", "azuread_application_certificate", } # A real Terraform or OpenTofu plan carries format_version, and omits # resource_changes entirely when there is nothing to change. tf_plan(p) if { is_object(p) p.format_version } standard_plan if { not input.plan.is_run_all tf_plan(input.plan) } run_all_plan if { input.plan.is_run_all == true is_object(input.plan.modules) count(input.plan.modules) > 0 every _, m in input.plan.modules { tf_plan(m) } } resource_changes := object.get(input.plan, "resource_changes", []) if standard_plan resource_changes := [rc | some _, m in input.plan.modules some rc in object.get(m, "resource_changes", []) ] if run_all_plan deny contains msg if { not standard_plan not run_all_plan msg := "Unsupported plan format for the credential policy" } deny contains msg if { some rc in resource_changes key_resources[rc.type] "create" in rc.change.actions msg := sprintf("%s: long-lived credential prohibited", [rc.address]) } allow if count(deny) == 0

The policy reads a standard Terraform or OpenTofu plan, or the module map from Terragrunt run-all. A plan with no changes can omit resource_changes , so an empty plan counts as valid, while an unrecognized shape is denied rather than silently allowed; attach it only to projects whose templates produce these formats, since Pulumi, CloudFormation, and Kubernetes deployments would all be denied. Replacements include a create action, so they’re caught. The resource list is an example, and the policy can’t see a hardcoded secret or a key generated outside Terraform.

The allow rule matters: with it, anything not denied proceeds without manual approval; without it, a policy that returns nothing defaults to pending, and every deployment waits for a person. Test with the full env zero input wrapper, not bare terraform show -json output, covering key creation, role-only plans, replacements, run-all, missing plan data, and destroys. ENV0_PRINT_POLICY_INPUT=true logs the exact input; ENV0_OPA_VERSION pins the OPA version. The policy runs on env zero’s default OPA (0.46.1) and on 1.x, which is why it uses future.keywords imports instead of import rego.v1 .

If an integration genuinely needs a persistent key, don’t just create it in another project. Use a documented exception: a named owner, a specific workload, least privilege, a revocation deadline, secure storage, monitoring, and an approval record. IAM access keys can’t be tagged, so record ownership on the identity and in your credential inventory.

## 3. Make sure you give every key a finite lifespan

AWS doesn’t give IAM user access keys an expiration date, so the end date has to come from somewhere else. For Terraform-managed credentials, an environment TTL gives you a teardown point: put disposable credentials in the same environment as what they serve and set a TTL. But a TTL isn’t credential expiry.

It starts a destroy, and the key disappears only if Terraform manages it and the destroy succeeds. A failed destroy, a locked environment, a manually created key, or an identity managed elsewhere leaves access behind, so verify revocation instead of trusting the countdown. TTLs can be extended or set to infinite, and TTL limits don’t bind admins . On the Free plan, once an organization passes 250 runs in a month, TTLs are destroyed; wait for the count to reset at the start of the next month (UTC), so a key can outlive its TTL by up to a month.

# What Kubernetes’ “monolith” lesson means for AI agent harnesses

Welcome to another edition of Road to KubeCon , your source for everything Kubernetes and cloud-native as we count down the days to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , happening November 9-12 in Salt Lake City, Utah.

This week, we take a look at the state of agent harnesses and what needs to evolve. We also feature HPE’s thoughts on Kubernetes visibility, more sci-fi agentic DevOps, and an impressive scheduler that shows Kubernetes’ default scheduler who’s the boss of GPU utilization.

That plus news from CNCF: what to expect at this year’s ArgoCon, a great opportunity to improve your open source project’s security hygiene, Atlassian’s stack for slashing event-to-metric latency, and a special gift for TNS readers.

## HPE shares tips for Kubernetes visibility on TNS

Getting Kubernetes running is a milestone. Knowing who owns the next upgrade, the access request, or failed recovery is an ongoing journey.

This week, we published “ A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap ,” the second installment in Chris J. Preimesberger’s four-part, HPE-sponsored series. It examines how platform and application teams divide responsibilities after launch, from configuration drift and security policies to upgrade validation and recovery drills. A healthy cluster doesn’t necessarily mean a healthy application — and someone needs to own that gap.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments.

Missed the opener? Part one explores Kubernetes self-service : how developers can get approved environments without waiting through ticket queues, while platform teams retain responsibility for access, costs, and lifecycle controls. Together, the articles ask a practical question: How do you give developers more independence while making operational accountability clear?

Next, the series turns to diagnosing slow applications when Kubernetes looks healthy, then to measuring AI inference performance. Both will explore the visibility teams need as their workloads become more demanding on the road to KubeCon.

## CNCF offers a 10% discount to TNS readers

This week, The New Stack readers get a special treat from Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). If you’re planning to attend KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA in Salt Lake City, use the discount code KCNA26MED10 when you register at this link for 10% off your admission.

We’re only 38 days out til KubeCon (or four Road to KubeCon editions out if you count in columns), so better act soon to register and plan your trip.

## Agent harnesses go cloud-native

The agent “harness” quickly became a catch-all for everything that surrounds an AI agent: the context, filesystem, subagents, permissions, and more. However, Craig McLuckie , founder and CEO of Stacklok , says it’s not enough.

To him, most harnesses are too local and built to serve a single developer at a laptop. The typical harness doesn’t scale well enough to serve hundreds of sessions. Sessions break, and you can’t easily move the experience between clients or devices.

This week, he takes to the CNCF blog to argue for a cloud-native agent harness. To him, that’s a distributed application that separates the agent loop from the infrastructure and services around it.

“Kubernetes taught this industry that a monolith in a container is still a monolith,” he writes. “The lesson applies to agents too.”

## Koordinator boosts on-Kubernetes GPU allocation >95%

A case study published on Tuesday details how Zhuoyu Technology, a Chinese autonomous driving technology company, is dramatically improving Kubernetes utilization with Koordinator , a CNCF sandbox project for efficiently scheduling microservices, AI, and big data workloads.

Zhuoyu Technology runs autonomous driving workloads on Kubernetes-based environments but hit performance inefficiencies with the default Kubernetes scheduler, which capped allocation and utilization. By using Koordinator, the team pushed GPU allocation above 95% and overall GPU utilization above 55%.

The case study demonstrates how certain gaps in the default Kubernetes scheduler can lead to failed launches, low GPU utilization, stranded GPUs, and distributed-job scheduling problems. It also demonstrates how Koordinator is faring well in production environments.

## CNCF and OpenSSF announce month-long challenge

Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) and CNCF are teaming up to organize the Security Slam , a 30-day challenge that walks participants through using OpenSSF projects to improve their project’s security posture.

All open source projects are invited to participate. Write Eddie Knight and OpenSSF’s Stacey Potter , the Slam is “now taking advantage of new tools to greatly broaden the qualifications for participation.”

The challenge runs October 5 through November 6. Register here to get involved and follow the objectives as they’re announced. Complete the challenges, and you might just have a fancy award ready for you at the OpenSSF booth (#313) at KubeCon.

## Atlassian’s cloud-native stack takes event-to-metric below 10 seconds

In incident detection and response, every second counts. On Wednesday, Deepak Biswas , senior engineering manager at Atlassian, shared a deep case study on the CNCF blog about Atlassian’s journey to show how far you can go to shave those seconds down.

The detection platform behind AutoHOT, its automated incident creation system, combines OpenTelemetry , Apache Kafka , and Apache Flink on Kubernetes. Operational telemetry tracks user actions across more than 10 cloud products serving millions of tenants, generating billions of events per day.

The headline says it all: They’ve reduced their event-to-metric metric (to be meta about it) from more than 40 seconds to under 10.

Yet, Biswas is honest: “It is not a success story with a bow on it.” They’re still working on fine-tuning. Recall, for instance, fell to 64% in August. Nevertheless, it’s a useful blueprint for others building automated incident detection and response workflows.

As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation.

## Argo CD 4.0 visioning begins

KubeCon NA will feature ArgoCon North America 2026 on the co-located day, Monday, Nov. 9. It’s a full-day, two-track event with practical ideas on improving software delivery, managing data and machine learning pipelines, and implementing progressive delivery.

In a post on the CNCF blog on Wednesday , ArgoCon co-chairs Dan Garfield, Christian Hernandez, and Katie Lamkin stress that the event comes as the community begins the visioning process for Argo CD 4.0.

They describe ArgoCon, whose schedule is live here , as “an opportunity to connect around what users are building today and where the projects are heading next.”

## Cycle’s DevOps control plane gets sci-fi

“If you told me this existed just a couple of years ago, I would have thought ‘this is science fiction, and it shouldn’t be real,'” says head of engineering Alexander Mattoni in a feature announcement video this week, showing off a new remote MCP server for Cycle, the DevOps control plane.

The release essentially means Cycle users can provision, orchestrate, and manage workloads across multicloud and hybrid environments via natural language, using MCP-compatible AI assistants and coding tools.

It follows a string of agentic features being released in the cloud native industry that continue to abstract DevOps and put impressive capabilities into the prompt. What was sci-fi yesterday is becoming more and more the status quo today.

We’ll be here every Friday to track it on The New Stack until KubeCon NA.

# Perplexity’s AI agents helped build a database. They weren’t allowed to run it.

Perplexity decided it was paying too much for DynamoDB and wasn’t getting the control it wanted over read performance. So it built its own database: CobbleDB.

Built by two engineers in two months with help from hundreds of persistent coding agents throughout development, CobbleDB is a roughly 40,000-line Rust key-value store that now handles part of Perplexity’s production search traffic. The company measured median batch-read latency at 5.6 milliseconds after the move, compared with 31.4 ms on DynamoDB before the cutover, while p99 went from 123 ms to 24.2 ms.

It’s expected to cost at least 20% less than DynamoDB and plans to open-source the database at some point.

But the database itself is only part of the story. CMU professor Andy Pavlo argued at Percona Live earlier this year that databases are the hardest and most important challenge for AI agents , in part because mistakes involving production data can be difficult or impossible to reverse.

Perplexity went ahead and used hundreds of agents to help build one anyway, but they weren’t given the keys to production.

## Why DynamoDB couldn’t keep up

Each search requires the serving layer to retrieve pre-chunked passages and vector embeddings, with a single Search API call fetching 100 to 120 page keys in batches of 10 to 20. Each item averages about 50 KB.

DynamoDB gave Perplexity little control over how it handled reads, which meant a slow replica could hold up the entire things. It also charged for the steady flow of large reads and writes generated by search, crawling, and reprocessing, which made cloud costs difficult to justify as traffic and the corpus grew.

That led Perplexity to separate long-term document storage from the database serving live searches.

## Three tiers for search data

The storage stack is split into three pieces. Pillar keeps durable document state in YTsaurus on HDDs, including versioned metadata, chunks and embeddings, while Lorry packages updates into partition-specific batches and moves them through S3 to CobbleDB.

Processed page data is spread across three replicas per partition, with hashed URLs as keys and RocksDB keeping often accessed data in memory while the rest stays on local NVMe. Reads stay within the same availability zone when possible, and the router can try another replica if one is slow rather than hold up the batch.

Updates come through S3 and are applied independently, allowing a replica to fall behind and catch up without blocking the others.

## Roughly 5X Lower Batch-Read Latency

Perplexity was handling approximately 200,000 requests per second when it measured CobbleDB at 5.6 ms for a median batch read, down from the 31.4 ms it had recorded on DynamoDB. At p99, latency went from 123 ms to 24.2 ms.

In later load testing, CobbleDB reached 500,000 requests per second before performance started to decline.

The comparison comes with an important caveat; DynamoDB and CobbleDB weren’t tested side by side against identical traffic: the DynamoDB figures were recorded before the cutover, and CobbleDB’s afterward. Perplexity separately ran synthetic benchmarks using batches of 10 to 15 keys with values ranging from 100 bytes to 100 KiB.

Its cost model puts CobbleDB at least 20% below DynamoDB across the commitment options evaluated, though that estimate doesn’t include the engineering cost of supporting the database.

## Agents built it, engineers controlled it

The agents carried context across sessions, catching problems with restore assumptions and runtime configuration while working on fixes and tests. But they weren’t running the database.

The two engineers kept control of the architecture and production system, particularly important given Pavlo’s warning about putting agents near critical production data.

## Ownership has long-term costs

Shipping CobbleDB in eight weeks solved Perplexity’s immediate engineering bottleneck, but maintaining a custom datastore could prove considerably harder. The latency results aren’t from a controlled side-by-side benchmark, and the projected savings don’t include the engineers needed to maintain CobbleDB and respond when something breaks.

Like Shopify and Ramp, which built custom coding agents around third-party models , Perplexity kept the cloud infrastructure but replaced a managed service with something built for its own needs. CobbleDB shows how AI-assisted development is changing that calculation, making custom infrastructure more practical for smaller engineering teams.
